items.title: The Rashtrakutas (c.753–973 CE)
items.body:
### The Rashtrakutas

**In one line**
The Rashtrakutas were a Deccan dynasty (based in modern Karnataka/Maharashtra) who rose from being junior officers of the Chalukyas to become the strongest power in India for about 200 years.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC likes the Rashtrakutas for two things the Deccan is famous for — the rock-cut **Kailasa temple at Ellora** and early **Kannada literature** — and for the way a small vassal family grew into an empire.

**The story (how a vassal family became an empire)**
A *feudatory* (a local chief who serves and pays a bigger king) named **Dantidurga** was serving the Badami Chalukya king **Kirtivarman II**. Around 753 CE he overthrew his overlord and set up his own kingdom — this is the start of the Rashtrakutas. His successor **Krishna I** finished off the remaining Chalukya lands and ordered the astonishing **Kailasa (Kailashnatha) temple at Ellora**, cut downwards out of one single hill of rock. Later, **Govinda III** became the greatest soldier of the line, raiding from the far south (Kanyakumari) all the way north to Kanauj and defeating the Pratihara king **Nagabhatta II**. The long-reigning **Amoghavarsha I** then chose peace and culture: he moved the capital to **Manyakheta (Malkhed)**, wrote the **Kavirajamarga** (the earliest surviving book of Kannada poetics) and leaned towards **Jainism** under the monk **Jinasena**. The last strong king, **Krishna III**, beat the Cholas and took Tanjore and Kanchi before the dynasty faded.

**Picture it (rulers in order)**

| Order | Ruler | Remembered for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Dantidurga | Founder (c.753); overthrew Kirtivarman II |
| 2 | Krishna I | Kailasa temple, Ellora |
| 3 | Govinda III | Greatest conqueror; beat Nagabhatta II |
| 4 | Amoghavarsha I | Manyakheta capital; Kavirajamarga; Jainism |
| 5 | Krishna III | Last strong king; took Tanjore & Kanchi |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory / vassal:** a local ruler who accepts a greater king as his master and pays him tribute.
- **Rock-cut monolith:** a building carved out of one solid piece of natural rock, not built from separate stones.
- **Kavirajamarga:** 'the royal road of poets' — the oldest known work on writing poetry in Kannada.

**How the Kailasa temple was made**
It was carved **top-down** from a single block of rock (a monolith) — workers cut away the hill from above, leaving the temple standing. Its style is **Dravidian (South Indian)**: the tiered tower over the shrine (the shikhara/vimana) resembles the Pallava **rathas at Mamallapuram**.

**Rashtrakuta literature (who wrote what)**

| Work | Author | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kavirajamarga | Amoghavarsha I | Earliest Kannada poetics |
| Adipurana | Jinasena | Lives of Jain saints (Sanskrit) |
| Vikramarjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bharata) | Pampa | Greatest Kannada poet |
| Santipurana | Ponna | Kannada poet, court of Krishna III |

**The three Chalukya branches**

| Branch | Capital / region |
| --- | --- |
| Chalukyas of Badami (early Western) | Vatapi (Badami) |
| Western Chalukyas (later Chalukyas) | Kalyani |
| Eastern Chalukyas | Vengi (coastal Andhra) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Kailasa temple at Ellora (Rashtrakuta, Krishna I)** is different from the **Kailasa/Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram (Pallava)** — same name, different builders and places.
- **Govinda III** = the most militarily successful Rashtrakuta monarch — his conquests extended from Kanyakumari to Kanauj (Kanyakubja), and he defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara king Nagabhatta II.
- **Manyakheta** was the Rashtrakuta capital; **Badami/Vatapi** was the earlier Chalukya capital they replaced.

**Remember it**
'DKG-AK' = **D**antidurga → **K**rishna I → **G**ovinda III → **A**moghavarsha I → (**K**rishna III). The Arab merchant **Suleman** ranked Amoghavarsha among the four greatest kings of the world.

**TL;DR**
- Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas (c.753) by overthrowing Chalukya Kirtivarman II.
- Krishna I built the rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora.
- Govinda III was the greatest conqueror (Kanyakumari to Kanauj; beat Nagabhatta II).
- Amoghavarsha I: Manyakheta capital, wrote Kavirajamarga, favoured Jainism.
- Pampa (greatest Kannada poet) wrote Vikramarjuna Vijaya; Bharuch was the main trade port.
keyPoints: Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas (c.753 CE) by overthrowing Chalukya Kirtivarman II; they were earlier Chalukya feudatories.
Krishna I built the rock-cut monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved top-down.
Govinda III was the greatest military ruler; conquests from Kanyakumari to Kanauj.
Amoghavarsha I shifted the capital to Manyakheta, wrote Kavirajamarga, and turned to Jainism under Jinasena.
Pampa (greatest Kannada poet) wrote Vikramarjuna Vijaya; Bharuch was the key Rashtrakuta trade port.
Literature: Kavirajamarga (Amoghavarsha I), Adipurana (Jinasena), Vikramarjuna Vijaya (Pampa), Santipurana (Ponna).
Chalukya branches: Badami = Vatapi; Western (later) Chalukyas = Kalyani; Eastern Chalukyas = Vengi (coastal Andhra).

items.title: Imperial Cholas — Major Rulers
items.body:
### Imperial Cholas — the great emperors

**In one line**
The Imperial Cholas (9th–13th centuries, Tamil Nadu) were the strongest South Indian empire and the greatest sea power India had seen, reaching from the Ganga to Southeast Asia.

**Why it is asked**
Two Chola achievements come up again and again: the **Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur** and the **naval expeditions** across the Bay of Bengal. Examiners test which king did which.

**The story (two kings you must separate)**
**Rajaraja I** (ruled 985–1014, born Arumolivarman) was the empire-builder. He conquered the Pandyas, parts of Kerala and northern **Ceylon (Sri Lanka)**, annexed the **Maldives**, and crowned his reign by building the towering **Brihadeeswara (Rajarajeswara) temple at Thanjavur**, consecrated in 1009–10. His son **Rajendra I** (1014–1044) then went further than any Indian king before him: he marched his army north, defeated the Pala king **Mahipala** and reached the **river Ganga**, taking the proud title **Gangaikondachola** ('the Chola who took the Ganga') and building a new capital, **Gangaikondacholapuram**. Most remarkably, his **navy crossed the sea and attacked the Srivijaya empire** (in modern Sumatra and Java) to protect the trade route to China, to which he also sent envoys. Later, **Virarajendra** beat the Chalukyas, and **Kulottunga I** (1070–1122) peacefully **joined the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (coastal Andhra) to the Cholas**, earning the title **Sungam tavirtta** ('he who abolished tolls') for scrapping internal trade taxes.

**Picture it (ruler → signature act)**

| Ruler | Reign | Signature act |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rajaraja I | 985–1014 | Thanjavur temple; Ceylon & Maldives |
| Rajendra I | 1014–1044 | Gangaikonda title; navy to Srivijaya |
| Kulottunga I | 1070–1122 | United Vengi & Cholas; abolished tolls |

**Terms explained**
- **Vimana:** the pyramid-shaped tower built over the main shrine in a South Indian (Dravidian) temple.
- **Srivijaya:** a powerful Southeast Asian maritime empire based in Sumatra (and spread over the Malay Peninsula) that controlled the sea route to China.
- **Toll (sungam):** a tax collected on goods moving through a region; abolishing it boosted trade.

**Don't confuse**
- **Rajaraja I = Thanjavur temple**; **Rajendra I = Gangaikondacholapuram temple + navy**. Both are called 'Brihadisvara', so link each to its town.
- **Mahipala** here is the **Pala** king of Bengal, not a Pratihara ruler.

**Remember it**
'Raja builds, Rajendra sails' — Rajaraja I built the Thanjavur temple; Rajendra I built the navy and the Ganga-title capital.

**TL;DR**
- Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur and conquered Ceylon and the Maldives.
- Rajendra I took the title Gangaikondachola after beating Pala king Mahipala, and built Gangaikondacholapuram.
- Rajendra I's navy invaded Srivijaya (Sumatra/Java); the Cholas sent missions to China.
- Kulottunga I united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas and abolished tolls.
- The Cholas were the dominant maritime power of the Bay of Bengal.
keyPoints: Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur and conquered Ceylon and the Maldives.
Rajendra I took the title Gangaikondachola after defeating Pala king Mahipala and built Gangaikondacholapuram.
Rajendra I's navy invaded Srivijaya (Sumatra/Java); Cholas sent missions to China.
Kulottunga I united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas and abolished tolls (Sungam tavirtta).
The Cholas were the dominant maritime power of the Bay of Bengal.

items.title: Chola Local Self-Government & Village Types
items.body:
### Chola village self-government

**In one line**
The Cholas ran their villages through elected assemblies and committees — one of the earliest documented systems of local self-government anywhere in the world.

**Why it is asked**
This is a favourite because it shows democracy at the village level centuries before modern times, and because the evidence comes from one famous set of inscriptions.

**The story (how a village governed itself)**
Most of what we know is carved on the walls of a temple at **Uttaramerur**, in inscriptions of the Chola king **Parantaka I** (around 919–921 CE). They describe how a village was split into **thirty wards (kudumbus)**. Each ward put forward candidates who met rules on age, honesty and property. The final members were then picked **by lot**, using the **kudavolai** ('pot-ticket') method — names written on palm-leaf tickets were drawn from a pot — and they served for just **one year**, so no one could cling to power. Day-to-day work was shared among specialist **committees (variyams)**: an annual committee, a garden committee, a tank (irrigation) committee and a gold committee. The village assembly, the **sabha**, owned the common land, decided and collected the land tax, and could even grant or cancel taxes.

**Picture it (the three kinds of village)**

| Village type | What it was |
| --- | --- |
| Ur | Ordinary village of mixed castes paying land revenue to the king (most common) |
| Brahmadeya (agrahara) | Land granted tax-free (tax-exempt) to Brahmins; usually prosperous |
| Devadana | Village granted to a temple, with its revenue given to the temple |

**Terms explained**
- **Inscription:** words carved on stone or metal; our main evidence for this period.
- **Kudavolai:** the 'pot-ticket' lottery used to choose committee members fairly.
- **Variyam:** a committee of the village assembly handling one job (gardens, tanks, and so on).
- **Sabha:** the assembly of a Brahmadeya village; the larger gathering was the mahasabha.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ur** = ordinary mixed village; **Sabha** = assembly of a Brahmin (Brahmadeya) village. Different bodies, often mixed up.
- **Uttaramerur** records the system; it was not a separate kingdom.

**Remember it**
'U-B-D' = **U**r (all castes) → **B**rahmadeya (Brahmins) → **D**evadana (deity/temple). Members were chosen by **pot-ticket** for **one year**.

**TL;DR**
- The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I record early Chola local self-government.
- Members were chosen from 30 wards by the kudavolai (lot/pot-ticket) system for one year.
- Committees (variyams) ran annual, garden, tank and gold affairs.
- Ur = ordinary revenue-paying village; Brahmadeya = tax-free Brahmin grant; Devadana = temple grant.
- The sabha owned common land and controlled the land tax — it had proprietary rights over communal village land and collected land revenue.
keyPoints: Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I record early Chola local self-government.
Village committee members were chosen from 30 wards by the kudavolai (lot/pot-ticket) system for one year.
Key committees: annual (samvatsaravariyam), garden (tottavariyam), tank (eri-variyam).
Ur = ordinary revenue-paying mixed-caste village; Brahmadeya = tax-free Brahmin grant.
Devadana = village granted to a temple, with revenues donated to it.

items.title: Chola Art — Temples & Bronzes
items.body:
### Chola art — temples and bronzes

**In one line**
The Cholas perfected the South Indian (Dravidian) temple and the art of casting bronze idols, leaving monuments now protected by UNESCO.

**Why it is asked**
Art and architecture questions are easy marks if you know the three UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' and the famous **Nataraja** bronze.

**The story (stone and metal)**
Chola temples grew taller and grander over time. **Rajaraja I** built the **Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur** with a soaring **vimana** (the pyramid tower over the shrine); its height is about 59.8 metres and it is nicknamed **Dakshina Meru** ('the Meru mountain of the south'). His son **Rajendra I** built a matching **Brihadisvara at Gangaikondacholapuram**, and later **Rajaraja II** built the elegant **Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram**. Together these three form the UNESCO **Great Living Chola Temples**. In metalwork the Cholas mastered the **lost-wax (cire-perdue)** casting method, and the finest result is the **Nataraja** — Shiva dancing inside a ring of fire — the signature image of the age.

**Picture it (the three UNESCO temples)**

| Temple | Place | Builder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brihadisvara | Thanjavur | Rajaraja I (vimana about 59.8 m) |
| Brihadisvara | Gangaikondacholapuram | Rajendra I (completed 1035) |
| Airavatesvara | Darasuram | Rajaraja II (chariot-style mandapa) |

**Terms explained**
- **Dravidian style:** the South Indian temple style with a pyramid **vimana** over the shrine, pillared halls (**mandapas**) and gateway towers (**gopuras**).
- **Lost-wax (cire-perdue) casting:** a bronze is first modelled in wax, covered in clay, the wax melted out, and molten metal poured into the gap.
- **Nataraja:** the form of Shiva as the cosmic dancer.

**Don't confuse**
- In the **Dravidian** style the tower over the shrine is the **vimana**; in the **Nagara (North Indian)** style it is the **shikhara**. The tall gateway is the **gopura**.
- **Thanjavur** and **Gangaikondacholapuram** both have a 'Brihadisvara' — tie each to its builder.

**Remember it**
Three temples, three builders: Thanjavur (Rajaraja I), Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I), Darasuram (Rajaraja II). Bronze icon = Nataraja.

**TL;DR**
- The three UNESCO Great Living Chola Temples: Thanjavur (Rajaraja I), Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I), Darasuram (Rajaraja II).
- Thanjavur's Brihadisvara is called Dakshina Meru; vimana about 59.8 m.
- Dravidian style = pyramidal vimana over the shrine, pillared mandapas, gopura gateways.
- The Cholas perfected lost-wax bronze casting; the Nataraja is the finest example.
- The Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram has a chariot-style mandapa.

items.title: The Kakatiyas of Warangal (1163–1323)
items.body:
### The Kakatiyas of Warangal

**In one line**
The Kakatiyas were the first great dynasty to politically unite the Telugu-speaking land (today's Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) under one rule, from their capital at Warangal.

**Why it is asked**
For APPSC this is core AP history: the Kakatiyas gave the Telugu region its first strong identity, its famous tank-irrigation and the UNESCO Ramappa temple.

**The story (rise, a queen, and the fall)**
Like many Deccan powers, the Kakatiyas began as **feudatories of the Western Chalukyas**. As Chalukya power weakened, **Prataparudra I (Rudradeva)** declared independence in **1163 CE**. The capital moved from **Hanumakonda** to the fort-city of **Warangal (Orugallu)** under **Ganapati Deva** (1198–1262), the dynasty's longest and strongest king, who united the Telugu territories, dug the great **Pakhal Lake** and issued the **Abhaya Sasanam** (a 'charter of safety') to invite traders to the port of **Motupalli**. His daughter **Rudrama Devi** (1262–1296) then became the **first woman to rule the dynasty**; she took a male royal title to command the nobles and so impressed the visiting Italian traveller **Marco Polo** that he praised her government. The end came under **Prataparudra II**: after repeated attacks from Delhi, **Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323**, and the Deccan lay open to the coming Bahmani Sultanate.

**Picture it (key rulers)**

| Ruler | Reign | Remembered for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prataparudra I | from 1163 | Declared independence from the Chalukyas |
| Ganapati Deva | 1198–1262 | Warangal capital; Pakhal Lake; Motupalli trade |
| Rudrama Devi | 1262–1296 | First woman ruler; praised by Marco Polo |
| Prataparudra II | 1296–1323 | Last ruler; Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs (1323) |

**Terms explained**
- **Orugallu:** the Telugu name of Warangal ('one stone'), after its great rock fort.
- **Abhaya Sasanam:** a royal charter promising safety and fair treatment to foreign merchants.
- **Tank:** a man-made reservoir that stores rain water for irrigation.

**Legacy (why the Kakatiyas still matter)**
- Their extensive **tank irrigation system** benefited the Telugu region for centuries.
- The **Ramappa (Rudreswara) Temple** at Palampet, built in their period, was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021**.
- Their **patronage of Telugu literature** laid a foundation for Telugu cultural identity.

**Don't confuse**
- **Prataparudra I** (declared independence, 1163) is a different king from **Prataparudra II** (the last ruler, fell 1323).
- **Rudrama Devi** (Kakatiya queen) is not the same as the earlier **Rudradeva** (Prataparudra I).

**Remember it**
Kakatiya = 'women and waters' — **Rudrama** the queen, **Pakhal & Ramappa** the tanks, **Warangal** the fort. Fell to the **Tughlaqs in 1323**.

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiyas ruled the Telugu region from Warangal; Prataparudra I declared independence from the Chalukyas in 1163.
- Ganapati Deva shifted the capital to Warangal, built Pakhal Lake, and issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam.
- Rudrama Devi was the first woman ruler, praised by Marco Polo.
- Prataparudra II was the last ruler; Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323.
- Ramappa Temple (Palampet) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021; tank irrigation was a key legacy.
keyPoints: Kakatiyas ruled Telugu regions from Warangal; Prataparudra I declared independence from the Chalukyas in 1163.
Ganapati Deva shifted the capital to Warangal, built Pakhal Lake, and issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam.
Rudrama Devi was the first woman ruler, praised by Marco Polo.
Prataparudra II was defeated and Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323, ending the dynasty.
Ramappa Temple (Palampet) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021; tank irrigation was a key legacy.

items.title: Hoysalas & Yadavas of the Deccan
items.body:
### Hoysalas and Yadavas

**In one line**
The Hoysalas (Karnataka) and the Yadavas of Devagiri (Maharashtra) were two Deccan dynasties that broke free of the Chalukyas, flowered in art and language, and were finally swallowed by the Delhi Sultanate.

**Why it is asked**
The Hoysalas are tested for their star-shaped soapstone temples at **Belur and Halebidu**; the Yadavas for being the **first to make Marathi an official language** and for the **Hemadpanti** building style.

**The story (two neighbours, similar fates)**
The **Hoysalas** rose as Western Chalukya feudatories. **Vishnuvardhana** (1108–1152) won independence by defeating the **Cholas** and seizing **Gangavadi**; influenced by the saint **Ramanujacharya**, he turned to Vaishnavism and built the **Chennakesava temple at Belur**. His capitals were **Belur** and **Halebidu (Dorasamudra)**. The dynasty's end came when **Veera Ballala III** was killed in the **Battle of Madurai (1343)**, and the Hoysala lands flowed into the rising **Vijayanagara empire**. The **Yadavas (Seunas)** ruled the northern Deccan from **Devagiri (Daulatabad)**. Their founder **Bhillama V** declared independence from the Chalukyas (around 1187), and the dynasty peaked under **Simhana II**. They were the first to use **Marathi as an official language** and produced scholars like **Hemadri**, the saint **Dnyaneshwar** and the music theorist **Sarangadeva**. Their end came from Delhi: **Malik Kafur**, general of **Alauddin Khalji**, defeated king **Ramachandra in 1308**; the kingdom was annexed by Delhi by **1317**, and the last Yadava ruler, **Harapaladeva**, was executed in **1318**.

**Picture it (compare the two)**

| Feature | Hoysalas | Yadavas (Seunas) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capital | Belur / Halebidu | Devagiri |
| Founder of independence | Vishnuvardhana | Bhillama V |
| Signature | Soapstone stellate temples | Marathi; Hemadpanti style |
| End | Ballala III, Madurai 1343 | Annexed by Delhi, 1317–18 |

**Terms explained**
- **Soapstone (chloritic schist):** a soft stone easy to carve in fine detail, used in Hoysala temples.
- **Jagati:** the raised star-shaped platform a Hoysala temple stands on.
- **Stellate plan:** a star-shaped ground plan, made by rotating a square.
- **Hemadpanti style:** a Yadava building style using black stone fitted without mortar (named after the minister Hemadri).

**Don't confuse**
- **Belur = Chennakesava temple (Vishnu)**; **Halebidu = Hoysaleswara temple (Shiva)**.
- **Battle of Madurai (1343)** ended the **Hoysalas**; do not mix it with the later Battle of Talikota (1565) that hurt Vijayanagara.

**Remember it**
Deccan pair — **Hoysala = soapstone stars at Belur/Halebidu**; **Yadava = Marathi at Devagiri**. Both fell to Delhi's Deccan campaigns.

**TL;DR**
- Vishnuvardhana founded Hoysala independence by defeating the Cholas; Belur and Halebidu were the capitals.
- Hoysala temples used soapstone, a jagati platform and a stellate (star) plan — Chennakesava (Belur), Hoysaleswara (Halebidu).
- Veera Ballala III died in the Battle of Madurai (1343); Hoysala lands merged with Vijayanagara.
- Yadavas (Seunas) ruled from Devagiri; Bhillama V founded the line and they first made Marathi an official language.
- Malik Kafur defeated Ramachandra in 1308; Delhi annexed the kingdom by 1317 (last ruler Harapaladeva executed 1318).

items.title: Shivaji & the Maratha State — Ashtapradhan, Revenue, Army
items.body:
### Shivaji and the Maratha state

**In one line**
Shivaji built a compact, well-run Deccan kingdom (Hindavi Swarajya) based on a salaried administration, hill forts and a navy, rather than on handing out land to nobles.

**Why it is asked**
Examiners test the eight-minister **Ashtapradhan** council and the two Maratha taxes, **Chauth** and **Sardeshmukhi**.

**The story (a kingdom run on cash, not land)**
**Shivaji** was crowned **Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674**. Unlike the Mughals, who paid nobles by granting them land, Shivaji mostly paid his officers and soldiers in **cash**, and kept their posts **non-hereditary**, so power stayed with the state. He was advised by a council of eight ministers, the **Ashtapradhan**, headed by the **Peshwa** (prime minister). To fund the state he levied **Chauth** and **Sardeshmukhi** — but, importantly, on lands **outside** his own kingdom (called **mulk-giri** raids into Mughal and other territory), sparing his core **swaraj** lands. **Chauth** was one-fourth (25%) of an area's assessed revenue, collected in return for protection; **Sardeshmukhi** was an extra one-tenth (10%), claimed because Shivaji called himself the hereditary chief headman (sardeshmukh) of Maharashtra. His army paired **bargirs** (cavalry given horses and gear by the state) with **silahdars** (who brought their own), and he is remembered as a pioneer of Indian naval defence, with sea-forts like **Sindhudurg** and **Vijaydurg**.

**Picture it (the two taxes)**

| Levy | Share | Why it was claimed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chauth | one-fourth (25%) | protection payment on lands outside swaraj |
| Sardeshmukhi | extra one-tenth (10%) | Shivaji as hereditary sardeshmukh of Maharashtra |

**Terms explained**
- **Swaraj vs mulk:** 'swaraj' = Shivaji's own core land; 'mulk' = outside territory raided for Chauth/Sardeshmukhi.
- **Ashtapradhan:** the council of eight ministers (ashta = eight, pradhan = minister).
- **Bargir / silahdar:** a state-equipped cavalryman / a self-equipped cavalryman.

**Don't confuse**
- **Chauth = 1/4**; **Sardeshmukhi = an extra 1/10**. Both fell on **outside (mulk)** lands, not on the core swaraj.
- The **Peshwa** under Shivaji was just the PM; only later did Peshwas become the real rulers of the Maratha state.

**Remember it**
'Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10' on **mulk** (outside) lands; the council is the **Ashtapradhan** (Peshwa = PM).

**TL;DR**
- Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674 and founded the Maratha (Hindavi Swarajya) state.
- Ashtapradhan = eight ministers; the Peshwa/Pantpradhan (prime minister, general administration), Amatya/Mujumdar (finance & accounts), Sumant/Dabir (foreign affairs), Nyayadhish (chief justice).
- Chauth (one-fourth) and Sardeshmukhi (extra one-tenth) were levied on external (mulk) lands, not on core swaraj.
- Shivaji kept a cash-paid standing army; bargirs used state horses while silahdars brought their own.
- He relied on hill-forts and built a navy (Sindhudurg), earning the tag 'father of the Indian navy'.

items.title: The Chalukyas of Badami (c.543–753 CE)
items.body:
### The Chalukyas of Badami (c.543–753 CE)

**In one line**
The Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) ruled the western Deccan from about 543 to 753 CE; their greatest king Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha, and their temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal are the starting point of Deccan temple art.

**The story**
The family rose in northern Karnataka. **Pulakeshin I** fortified **Vatapi** (Badami) and declared himself king. His grandson **Pulakeshin II** made the dynasty great: the **Aihole inscription** written by **Ravikirti** says he defeated **Harsha** on the **Narmada**. He fought the Pallavas of Kanchi for years, but in **642** the Pallava **Narasimhavarman I** captured Vatapi and killed him. His brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** had already set up a separate line at **Vengi** in coastal Andhra (624). **Vikramaditya I** won Vatapi back, **Vikramaditya II** occupied Kanchi, and the last king **Kirtivarman II** was overthrown by his feudatory **Dantidurga**, founder of the Rashtrakutas.

#### Rulers in order

| Ruler | Reign | Remembered for |
|---|---|---|
| **Pulakeshin I** | c.543–566 | Founder; fortified **Vatapi** (Badami); performed the ashvamedha |
| **Kirtivarman I** | 566–597 | Defeated the **Kadamba**s of Banavasi, the Nalas and the Mauryas of Konkan |
| **Mangalesha** | 597–610 | Completed the Badami caves; his inscription (578 CE) is in **Cave 3** (Vishnu cave) |
| **Pulakeshin II** | **610–642** | Greatest ruler; title **Dakshinapatheshvara** (lord of the south); see below |
| **Vikramaditya I** | 655–681 | **Recovered Vatapi** from the Pallavas and restored the kingdom |
| **Vikramaditya II** | 733–744 | Occupied the Pallava capital **Kanchi** and spared its temples; queens built Pattadakal temples |
| **Kirtivarman II** | 744–753 | **Last** ruler; overthrown by the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga (c.753) |

#### Pulakeshin II — the five facts asked

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Aihole inscription** (634 CE) | A Sanskrit eulogy composed by the Jain court poet **Ravikirti**, on the Meguti temple |
| **Victory over Harsha** | Defeated **Harsha**vardhana on the banks of the **Narmada** (c.618–619) — Harsha never crossed south of it |
| **Hiuen Tsang** | The Chinese pilgrim visited the kingdom of **Pulakeshin II** and praised its warlike people |
| **Persian embassy** | Exchanged envoys with the Persian king **Khusrau II**; an Ajanta Cave 1 painting is traditionally read as this embassy |
| **Death (642)** | Pallava **Narasimhavarman I** sacked Vatapi, killed Pulakeshin II and took the title **Vatapikonda** |
| **Eastern branch** | Pulakeshin II's brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** founded the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (**624** CE) |

#### Temples of the Badami Chalukyas

| Site / term | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Aihole** | '**Cradle** of Indian temple architecture' — ~120 early experimental temples (Ladkhan, apsidal Durga temple, Meguti Jain temple) |
| **Badami** (Vatapi) | **Four** rock-cut cave temples — three Brahmanical (Shiva, Vishnu) and one Jain |
| **Pattadakal** | UNESCO World Heritage Site (**1987**); the Chalukya coronation town on the Malaprabha |
| **Two styles together** | Pattadakal has **Nagara** (Papanatha, Galaganatha) and **Dravida** (Virupaksha, Mallikarjuna) temples side by side |
| **Virupaksha temple** | Built by Queen **Lokamahadevi** after Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas; modelled on the Kailasanatha of Kanchi |
| **Mallikarjuna temple** | Built by Queen **Trailokyamahadevi**, sister of Lokamahadevi |
| **Vesara** | The hybrid Deccan style mixing Nagara and Dravida features, developed by the Chalukyas |

**Terms explained**
- **Ashvamedha:** the horse sacrifice performed by a king to claim paramount power.
- **Feudatory:** a subordinate chief who serves and pays tribute to an overlord.

**Don't confuse**
- **Pulakeshin II** defeated **Harsha** (north, Narmada) but was killed by the Pallava **Narasimhavarman I** (south, 642).
- **Aihole** = the inscription of Ravikirti and the early experimental temples; **Pattadakal** = the mature temples and the UNESCO site.
- **Badami Chalukyas** (Vatapi) ≠ **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** (973–1189) ≠ **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (624–1070s).

**TL;DR**
- Pulakeshin I founded the line; Pulakeshin II (610–642) was the greatest.
- Aihole inscription (634) by Ravikirti: victory over Harsha on the Narmada.
- Narasimhavarman I (Pallava) took Vatapi in 642 — title Vatapikonda.
- Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Vengi line (624).
- Pattadakal (UNESCO 1987) has Nagara and Dravida temples; Virupaksha by Queen Lokamahadevi; Vesara = Deccan hybrid style.
keyPoints: Pulakeshin II (610–642): Aihole inscription by Ravikirti; defeated Harsha on the Narmada; killed when Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi (642).
Pulakeshin I founded the Badami Chalukyas and fortified Vatapi; Kirtivarman II was the last ruler.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakeshin II, founded the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in 624 CE.
Aihole = cradle of Indian temple architecture; Pattadakal (UNESCO 1987) mixes Nagara and Dravida temples.
Virupaksha temple (Pattadakal) was built by Queen Lokamahadevi; Vesara = the Deccan hybrid style.

items.title: Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973–1189) & Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
items.body:
### Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973–1189) & Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi

**In one line**
Two later Chalukya lines matter: the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, who replaced the Rashtrakutas in 973, and the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in coastal Andhra, who merged with the Cholas.

**The story**
In **973** the Chalukya chief **Tailapa II** overthrew the last Rashtrakuta, **Karka II**, and revived the Chalukya name. **Someshvara I** moved the capital to **Kalyani**, and under **Vikramaditya VI** the court produced two famous books: **Bilhana**'s life of the king and **Vijnaneshwara**'s **Mitakshara**, still the base of Hindu inheritance law. Kalyani's long wars with the Cholas exhausted it, and its feudatories — the Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas — took over in the 12th century. In the east, the **Vengi** line founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana married into the Chola family: **Rajaraja Narendra**, patron of the Telugu poet **Nannaya**, married a Chola princess, and his son became the Chola emperor **Kulottunga I**.

#### Western Chalukyas of Kalyani

| Ruler / figure | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Tailapa II** | 973–997 | Founder (**973**); overthrew the last Rashtrakuta, Karka II; patron of the poet Ranna |
| **Someshvara I** | 1042–1068 | Made **Kalyani** (Basavakalyan) the capital; lost to the Cholas at Koppam and Kudal Sangamam |
| **Vikramaditya VI** | 1076–1126 | Greatest ruler; started the **Chalukya-Vikrama era** (1076) |
| **Bilhana** | Court poet | Wrote the **Vikramankadevacharita**, the life of Vikramaditya VI |
| **Vijnaneshwara** | Jurist at Kalyani | Wrote the **Mitakshara** (on the Yajnavalkya Smriti) — the basis of Hindu inheritance law |
| **Someshvara III** | 1126–1138 | Wrote the **Manasollasa** (Abhilashitartha Chintamani), a royal encyclopaedia; called 'Sarvajna Chakravarti' |
| **Successor states** | 12th century | Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas all rose as **feudatories** of the Chalukyas of **Kalyani** |

#### Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Capital** | **Vengi** (Pedavegi, near **Eluru**); later Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry) |
| **Rajaraja Narendra** (1019–1061) | Patron of **Nannaya**, who began the Telugu **Andhra Mahabharatam**; ruled from Rajamahendravaram |
| **Chola marriage link** | Rajaraja Narendra married **Ammangadevi** (daughter of Rajendra I); their son became **Kulottunga I** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mitakshara** (Vijnaneshwara, Kalyani) is a law commentary; **Manasollasa** (Someshvara III) is an encyclopaedia.
- The **Chalukya-Vikrama era** (1076) is Vikramaditya VI's; it is not the Vikrama Samvat of 57 BCE.
- **Rajaraja Narendra** (Eastern Chalukya, Nannaya) ≠ **Rajaraja I** (Chola, Thanjavur).

**TL;DR**
- Tailapa II ended the Rashtrakutas in 973.
- Vikramaditya VI: Chalukya-Vikrama era; Bilhana and Vijnaneshwara (Mitakshara).
- Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas began as Kalyani feudatories.
- Vengi line: Nannaya under Rajaraja Narendra; Kulottunga I joined Vengi to the Cholas.
keyPoints: Tailapa II founded the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973) by overthrowing Karka II.
Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126): Chalukya-Vikrama era; Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita; Vijnaneshwara's Mitakshara.
Someshvara III wrote the Manasollasa; Someshvara I made Kalyani the capital.
Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi; Nannaya began the Andhra Mahabharatam under Rajaraja Narendra.
Rajaraja Narendra married Ammangadevi; their son Kulottunga I united Vengi with the Cholas.

items.title: Rashtrakutas — More Rulers, Ellora, Literature & Administration
items.body:
### Rashtrakutas — More Rulers, Ellora, Literature & Administration

**In one line**
Beyond the four famous kings, exams ask the northern raids (Dhruva, Indra III), the Battle of Takkolam, the layout of the Ellora caves and the "three gems" of Kannada.

**The story**
The Rashtrakutas (c.753–973) ruled from **Manyakheta** and fought on two fronts. In the north, **Dhruva** was the first to join the struggle for **Kanauj**, Govinda III repeated it, and **Indra III** actually sacked Kanauj in 916. In the south, **Krishna III** beat the Chola **Parantaka I** at **Takkolam** (949). Their cultural mark is at **Ellora**, where the **Kailasa** temple (Cave 16) stands among 34 Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, and in Kannada poetry, where **Pampa** opened the classical age. In 973 the last king, **Karka II**, lost the throne to **Tailapa II**.

#### More Rashtrakuta rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Dantidurga** | 735–756 | Founder; his inscription is in the **Dashavatara** cave (Cave 15), Ellora; his name means 'he whose elephant is his fort' |
| **Pallava alliance** | — | Dantidurga's daughter married the Pallava **Nandivarman II**; Dantidurga helped him regain Kanchi |
| **Dhruva Dharavarsha** | 780–793 | First to march north — defeated the Pratihara **Vatsaraja** and the Pala Dharmapala |
| **Amoghavarsha I** | **814–878** | Longest reign (~64 years); Manyakheta capital; Kavirajamarga; Jain leanings |
| **Prashnottara Ratnamalika** | — | A Sanskrit moral work also credited to Amoghavarsha I (translated into Tibetan) |
| **Indra III** | 914–929 | Sacked **Kanauj** (916), defeating the Pratihara Mahipala; the Arab al-Masudi visited |
| **Krishna III** | 939–967 | Last strong king; won the **Battle of Takkolam** (**949**) over the Chola Parantaka I and took Kanchi and Tanjore |
| **Karka II** | 972–973 | Last ruler; overthrown by **Tailapa II** of the Kalyani Chalukyas (973) |

#### Ellora and Elephanta

| Site | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Ellora caves** | **34** caves — 1–12 Buddhist, 13–29 Hindu, 30–34 **Jain**; UNESCO site (1983) |
| **Kailasa temple** | **Cave 16**; about 200 ft long and 100 ft wide and high; elephants and lions on the plinth seem to carry it |
| **Sculptures** | **Ravana** shaking Mount Kailasa; Durga slaying the buffalo demon; a hall of 16 square pillars |
| **Elephanta caves** | The three-headed **Mahesamurti** (Trimurti); credited to the Rashtrakutas (some say the **Kalachuri**s) |

#### Rashtrakuta-age literature

| Author / work | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Pampa** (Adikavi) | Kannada Adipurana; Vikramarjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bharata) — at the court of the feudatory Arikesari II |
| **Three gems of Kannada** | **Pampa**, **Ponna** (Shantipurana) and **Ranna** (Gadayuddha, at the Kalyani court) — the **three gems** (Ratnatraya) |
| **Ranna** | **Gadayuddha** — the mace duel of Bhima and Duryodhana; court of Tailapa II |
| **Mahaviracharya** | **Ganitasarasangraha**, a mathematics text (the source PDF calls him "Viracharya", work "Ganitasaram") |
| **Sakatayana** | **Amoghavritti**, a grammar named after Amoghavarsha |
| **Jinasena** | Adipurana and **Parshvabhyudaya** (life of Parshva in verse); guru of Amoghavarsha |

#### Administration, trade and foreign accounts

| Term | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Rashtra** / **vishaya** | Province (**rashtra**) under a rashtrapati → district (**vishaya**) under a vishayapati → bhukti → village |
| **Balhara** | The Arab name for the Rashtrakuta king (from **Vallabha**raja); Arab traders were welcomed |
| **Suleman** (851) | Ranked Amoghavarsha among the **four greatest** kings, with the Caliph, the Byzantine emperor and the Chinese emperor |
| **Bharuch** (Broach) | The chief port on the west coast, linking the Deccan to Arab trade |

**Don't confuse**
- **Takkolam (949)**: Rashtrakuta Krishna III beat Chola Parantaka I. Do not confuse with **Koppam (1054)**, a Chola–Kalyani Chalukya battle.
- **Ranna** wrote at the Kalyani Chalukya court of Tailapa II, though he is grouped with the Rashtrakuta-age poets Pampa and Ponna.
- **Ellora** has caves of three religions; **Ajanta** is purely Buddhist.

**TL;DR**
- Dhruva and Indra III (sacked Kanauj, 916) took the Rashtrakutas north.
- Krishna III won Takkolam (949); Karka II lost to Tailapa II (973).
- Ellora: 34 caves (Buddhist 1–12, Hindu 13–29, Jain 30–34); Kailasa = Cave 16.
- Pampa, Ponna, Ranna = the three gems of Kannada.
keyPoints: Krishna III defeated the Chola Parantaka I at Takkolam (949); Indra III sacked Kanauj (916).
Dhruva was the first Rashtrakuta to intervene in the north; Karka II, the last, fell to Tailapa II in 973.
Ellora has 34 caves — Buddhist, Hindu and Jain; the Kailasa temple is Cave 16.
Pampa (Adikavi), Ponna and Ranna are the three gems of Kannada; Mahaviracharya wrote Ganitasarasangraha.
Rashtras (provinces) and vishayas (districts); Arabs called the king Balhara; Bharuch was the chief port.

items.title: Cholas — Rulers, Titles, Battles, Administration & Literature
items.body:
### Cholas — Rulers, Titles, Battles, Administration & Literature

**In one line**
The Imperial Cholas (c.850–1279) have the longest king list in South India; exams pick the founder, the titles, a few battles, the administrative units and the Tamil classics of the age.

**The story**
**Vijayalaya** seized **Thanjavur** around 850, **Aditya I** ended the Pallavas, and **Parantaka I** took Madurai but lost to the Rashtrakutas at Takkolam. After a pause, **Rajaraja I** (Arumolivarman) built the empire — Ceylon, the Maldives, a navy — and **Rajendra I** carried it to the Ganga and to **Kadaram** in the Srivijaya empire. The Chalukya wars cost a king's life at **Koppam** (1054). **Kulottunga I**, half Eastern Chalukya, joined Vengi to the empire, and the empire lasted until **Rajendra III** (1279), when the **Pandyas** took over. The empire ran from **mandalams** down to self-governing villages, and Tamil literature peaked with **Kamban** and **Sekkilar**.

#### Chola rulers you must place

| Ruler | Reign | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Vijayalaya** | c.850–871 | Founder; took **Thanjavur** from the **Muttaraiyar**s; built a temple to Durga (Nisumbhasudini) |
| **Aditya I** | 871–907 | Defeated the Pallava **Aparajita**, ending Pallava rule in Tondaimandalam |
| **Parantaka I** | 907–955 | Took Madurai — title **Maduraikonda**; Uttaramerur inscriptions (919, 921); lost at Takkolam (949) |
| **Rajaraja I** | 985–1014 | Original name **Arumolivarman**; titles Mummudi Chola, Shivapadasekhara |
| **Rajadhiraja I** | 1044–1054 | Killed in the **Battle of Koppam** (**1054**) against the Chalukya Someshvara I |
| **Virarajendra** | 1063–1070 | Beat the Chalukyas (Kudal Sangamam); victory pillar on the **Tungabhadra**; patron of Buddhamitra |
| **Kulottunga I** | **1070–1122** | United Vengi and the Cholas; abolished tolls; re-surveyed land |
| **Rajaraja II** | 1146–1173 | Built the Airavatesvara temple at **Darasuram** |
| **Rajendra III** | 1246–1279 | Last Chola; the **Pandya**s of Madurai became the leading Tamil power |

#### Conquests, titles and foreign links

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Polonnaruva** | Capital of the Chola province in north Ceylon after Rajaraja I beat **Mahinda V** |
| **Maldives** | Annexed by Rajaraja I — part of his naval reach |
| **Kandalur Salai** | Rajaraja I destroyed the Chera fleet here — his first naval victory |
| **Chudamani Vihara** | Buddhist vihara at **Nagapattinam** (Negapatam) built by the Sailendra king of Srivijaya with Rajaraja I's support |
| **Kadaramkonda** | 'Conqueror of Kadaram' (Kedah, Malay Peninsula) — Rajendra I's title after the Srivijaya raid |
| **Ganga campaign (1022)** | Rajendra I beat the Pala king **Mahipala** in **1022** but annexed nothing in the north |
| **Chola-Pandya viceroyalty** | Pandya and Kerala country placed under a Chola prince with headquarters at **Madurai** |
| **China embassy** | Kulottunga I sent an embassy of **72 merchants** to China (1077) |
| **Loss of Ceylon** | King **Vijayabahu** I overthrew Chola rule in Ceylon in Kulottunga I's reign |
| **Land re-survey** | Kulottunga I's chief internal reform — a **re-survey** of land for tax purposes |

#### Administration and assemblies

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Mandalam** → **valanadu** → nadu → ur | Province → division → district → village; mandalams were often under princes |
| **Nagaram** | The assembly of **merchants** in a trading town |
| **Ur** | General assembly of an ordinary (**non-Brahmin**) village |
| **Sabha** / **mahasabha** | Assembly of a **Brahmadeya** (Brahmin-granted) village; its members were perunguri |
| **Chaturvedimangalam** | A large Brahmadeya settlement of Brahmins learned in the four Vedas (Uttaramerur was one) |
| **Uttaramerur** | A village in **Kanchipuram** district, Tamil Nadu — its temple walls carry the election rules |
| **30 wards** | Each of the **30 wards** (kudumbus) put up eligible candidates; one was drawn by lot (kudavolai) for one year |
| **Committees** | Annual (samvatsara-variyam, 12), garden (totta-variyam, 12), tank (**eri-variyam**, **six**), plus pancha-variyam and pon-variyam (gold) |
| **Perunguri** / variyapperumakkal | Members of the mahasabha / members of a committee; paid **madhyasthas** kept records |
| **Nyayattar** | The judicial committee of the village |
| **Devadana** trend | Temple-granted villages grew more **popular** because temples became the centre of village life |
| **Merchant guilds** | **Manigramam** and **Ayyavole** (Ainnurruvar, "the Five Hundred") traded across South-East Asia |

#### Tamil literature of the Chola age

| Author | Work |
|---|---|
| **Sekkilar** | **Periyapuranam** — lives of the 63 Shaiva Nayanars; court of Kulottunga II |
| **Kamban** | **Ramavataram** (Kamba Ramayanam), the Tamil Ramayana — 12th century (Kulottunga III, date debated) |
| **Jayamkondar** | **Kalingattupparani** — war poem on Kulottunga I's Kalinga campaign (general Karunakara Tondaiman) |
| **Buddhamitra** | **Virasoliyam** — Tamil grammar bringing it closer to Sanskrit; under Virarajendra; studied in Buddhist colleges |
| **Ottakuttan** | Court poet of three kings (Vikrama Chola, Kulottunga II, Rajaraja II); wrote the Muvar Ula |

**Terms explained**
- **Viceroyalty:** a province ruled by a deputy (often a prince) on the king's behalf.
- **Guild:** an association of merchants who traded together and protected their members.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ur** = assembly of an ordinary village; **sabha** = assembly of a Brahmadeya village; **nagaram** = merchants' assembly.
- **Takkolam (949)**: Rashtrakutas beat the Cholas; **Koppam (1054)**: Cholas vs Kalyani Chalukyas, Rajadhiraja I killed.
- **Kamban** = Ramayana; **Sekkilar** = Periyapuranam; **Jayamkondar** = Kalingattupparani.

**TL;DR**
- Vijayalaya founded the line (Thanjavur, c.850); Rajendra III was the last (1279).
- Parantaka I = Maduraikonda; Rajendra I = Gangaikondachola and Kadaramkonda.
- Mandalam → valanadu → nadu → ur; ur, sabha and nagaram assemblies.
- Kamban (Ramavataram), Sekkilar (Periyapuranam), Jayamkondar (Kalingattupparani).
keyPoints: Vijayalaya founded the Imperial Cholas by taking Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars (c.850).
Parantaka I took the title Maduraikonda; Rajadhiraja I died at Koppam (1054); Rajendra III was the last Chola.
Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam was built by the Sailendra king with Rajaraja I's support.
Empire: mandalam → valanadu → nadu → ur; ur = ordinary village assembly, sabha = Brahmadeya assembly, nagaram = merchants.
Sekkilar wrote the Periyapuranam; Kamban wrote the Ramavataram; Jayamkondar wrote the Kalingattupparani.

items.title: Chola Temples — Early Shrines and the UNESCO Trio in Detail
items.body:
### Chola Temples — Early Shrines and the UNESCO Trio in Detail

**In one line**
Chola temples grew from small early shrines at Narthamalai and Pullamangai to the giant Brihadisvara at Thanjavur; exams ask the nicknames, heights and UNESCO dates.

**The story**
The early Chola temples are small stone shrines. The **Vijayalaya Cholisvaram** at **Narthamalai** and the **Brahmapurisvara** at **Pullamangai** already show the wall niches and carved figures that later temples enlarged. Rajaraja I then built the Thanjavur temple, which its own inscriptions call **Dakshina Meru**; its gateway is the **Rajarajantiruvasal**. Rajendra I's temple at **Gangaikondacholapuram** is lower (53 m) and gently curved, and Rajaraja II's **Airavatesvara** at Darasuram turned the porch into a stone chariot — an idea Konark took further. UNESCO listed Thanjavur in **1987** and added the other two in **2004**.

#### Temple facts

| Temple / feature | Fact |
|---|---|
| **UNESCO listing** | Thanjavur inscribed **1987**; extended in **2004** to Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram |
| **Dakshina Meru** | Inscriptional name of the Thanjavur temple — 'Meru of the south'; consecrated 1010 |
| **Rajarajantiruvasal** | The main gopura (gateway) of the Thanjavur temple; the prakara has shrines of the ashtadikpalas |
| **Murals** | The inner walls carry Chola **mural** paintings |
| **Gangaikondacholapuram** | Completed 1035; **53**-m vimana with recessed corners and a graceful **curving** rise |
| **Darasuram** | 24-m vimana; mandapa shaped as a **chariot** with wheels — an idea later expanded at **Konark** (13th century) |
| **Vijayalaya Cholisvaram** | Early Chola temple at **Narthamalai**; faces west; Shiva shows the vismaya (wonder) gesture |
| **Brahmapurisvara** | Early Chola temple at **Pullamangai**; deities in wall niches; a figure riding a vyala (leogryph) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Dakshina Meru** = Thanjavur (Rajaraja I), not Gangaikondacholapuram.
- The chariot-shaped mandapa is at **Darasuram** (12th century); the full chariot temple is **Konark** (13th century, Eastern Ganga).

**TL;DR**
- Thanjavur = Dakshina Meru; UNESCO 1987, extended 2004.
- Gangaikondacholapuram: 53-m curving vimana (1035).
- Darasuram: chariot mandapa, precursor of Konark.
- Early shrines: Narthamalai, Pullamangai.
keyPoints: Great Living Chola Temples: Thanjavur inscribed 1987; extended 2004 to Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.
Thanjavur temple = Dakshina Meru; gateway = Rajarajantiruvasal; mural paintings on its walls.
Gangaikondacholapuram vimana is 53 m with a curving outline; Darasuram has a chariot-shaped mandapa (anticipates Konark).
Early Chola temples: Vijayalaya Cholisvaram (Narthamalai), Brahmapurisvara (Pullamangai).

items.title: Hoysalas & Yadavas — Rulers, Temples, Literature and the Fall to Delhi
items.body:
### Hoysalas & Yadavas — Rulers, Temples, Literature and the Fall to Delhi

**In one line**
The Hoysalas (Karnataka) and the Yadavas (Maharashtra) are tested on their founders, a few titles, the temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, their writers, and the Khalji raids that destroyed them.

**The story**
The Hoysala story starts with the legend of **Sala** striking a tiger. **Vishnuvardhana** won **Talakad** from the Cholas in 1116 and built the **Chennakesava** temple at Belur (1117); his official **Ketamalla** built the **Hoysaleswara** at Halebidu. **Narasimha III**'s general built the **Keshava** temple at **Somanathapura** (1268), and in **2023** UNESCO listed all three as the **Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas**. In Maharashtra, **Bhillama V** founded **Devagiri** in 1187 and **Simhana II** was the greatest Yadava. In **1296** Alauddin Khalji raided Devagiri — the first Turkish raid into the Deccan — and Malik Kafur finished the job: Ramachandra was captured (1308), Dwarasamudra sacked (1311), Shankaradeva killed (1313) and **Harapaladeva** executed (1318).

#### Hoysala rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Sala** | Legend | Legendary founder; killed a **tiger** at his Jain guru's call ('Hoy, Sala!' — 'Strike, Sala!'); the scene is the royal emblem |
| **Vishnuvardhana** (Bittideva) | 1108–1152 | Title **Talakadugonda** after taking Talakad from the Cholas (**1116**); Jain turned Vaishnava under Ramanuja |
| **Bittideva** | — | The name of Vishnuvardhana before his conversion to Vaishnavism |
| **Shantala Devi** | — | Vishnuvardhana's queen — a famed dancer who stayed a Jain |
| **Veera Ballala II** | 1173–1220 | Most powerful Hoysala; fought the Yadavas and Pandyas; patron of **Janna**, Nemichandra and Rudrabhatta |
| **Narasimha III** | 1263–1292 | Keshava temple at **Somanathapura** (**1268**), built by his general Somanatha |
| **Veera Ballala III** | 1292–1343 | Malik Kafur sacked **Dwarasamudra** (Halebidu) in **1311**; he died at Madurai in 1343 |

#### Hoysala temples, features and writers

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Hoysaleswara**, Halebidu | Twin Shiva temple (c.1121) built by **Ketamalla**, an official of Vishnuvardhana (the PDF credits the king) |
| **Chennakesava**, Belur | **1117**; also called Vijayanarayana — commemorates the victory over the Cholas; lathe-turned pillars |
| **Lathe-turned pillars** | Polished, ring-shaped pillars turned on a lathe — a Hoysala signature |
| **UNESCO 2023** | '**Sacred Ensembles** of the Hoysalas' — Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in **2023** (45th session, Riyadh) |
| **Administrative units** | Nadu, vishaya, **kampana** and desha |
| **Janna** | **Yashodharacharite** (Kannada) |
| **Harihara** | **Girijakalyana** — marriage of Shiva and Parvati |
| **Rudrabhatta** | **Jagannatha Vijaya** — Krishna's battle with Banasura |

#### Yadava (Seuna) rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Dridhaprahara** | Early | Early/legendary founder of the Seuna family (the PDF table names him founder; its text names Bhillama V) |
| **Bhillama V** | c.1173–1191 | Declared independence (**1187**), founded Devagiri, took the Chalukya capital Kalyani; fought Hoysala Ballala II |
| **Simhana II** | c.1210–1247 | **Greatest** Yadava; defeated the Shilahara Bhoja II of Kolhapur; patron of Sarangadeva |
| **Ramachandra** | 1271–1311 | Alauddin Khalji raided **Devagiri** in **1296** (first raid into the Deccan); Malik Kafur captured him in 1308; title Rai Rayan |
| **Shankaradeva** (Simhana III) | 1311–1313 | Stopped tribute; killed by Malik Kafur (**1313**) |
| **Harapaladeva** | 1317–1318 | Last Yadava; executed under **Mubarak** Shah Khalji (1318); kingdom annexed |

#### Yadava literature and architecture

| Author / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Sarangadeva** | **Sangita Ratnakara** — standard text of Indian music (the PDF also spells him "Sarangapani") |
| **Hemadri** (Hemadpant) | Minister; wrote the **Chaturvarga Chintamani** (a dharma encyclopaedia; the PDF calls it "Chaturanga Chintamani"); the Hemadpanti style is named after him |
| **Dnyaneshwar** | **Dnyaneshwari** (**1290**, Nevasa) — Marathi commentary on the Gita |
| **Mukundaraja** | **Vivekasindhu** — early Marathi philosophical work |
| **Mhaimbhat** | **Lilacharitra** — life of Chakradhar (Mahanubhava sect), early Marathi prose |
| **Hemadpanti style** | Local black stone fitted without **mortar** |
| **Gondeshwar temple**, **Sinnar** | Bhumija style; panchayatana layout (main shrine + four smaller shrines) |

**Don't confuse**
- **1296** = Alauddin's own raid on Devagiri (as Jalaluddin's governor); **1308** = Malik Kafur captures Ramachandra.
- **Sangita Ratnakara** (Sarangadeva, music) ≠ **Chaturvarga Chintamani** (Hemadri, dharma).
- Hoysala UNESCO listing is **2023**; the Kakatiya Ramappa temple was listed in **2021**.

**TL;DR**
- Sala tiger legend; Vishnuvardhana = Talakadugonda; Chennakesava 1117.
- Somanathapura Keshava temple (1268, Narasimha III); UNESCO Sacred Ensembles 2023.
- Bhillama V founded Devagiri (1187); Simhana II greatest; Alauddin raided Devagiri in 1296.
- Sarangadeva, Hemadri, Dnyaneshwar (1290); Hemadpanti = black stone without mortar.
keyPoints: Sala (tiger legend) is the legendary Hoysala founder; Vishnuvardhana took the title Talakadugonda (1116).
Keshava temple, Somanathapura (1268) under Narasimha III; Hoysaleswara (Halebidu) built by Ketamalla.
UNESCO 2023: 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas' — Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura.
Bhillama V founded Devagiri (1187); Alauddin's raid on Devagiri (1296) was the first into the Deccan; Harapaladeva executed 1318.
Sarangadeva — Sangita Ratnakara; Hemadri — Chaturvarga Chintamani; Dnyaneshwar — Dnyaneshwari (1290).

items.title: For Mains — South Indian Dynasties
items.body:
### For Mains — South Indian Dynasties

Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-2) asks you to *analyse*, not list. Pick a lens — administration, art, economy or legacy — and argue it with named evidence.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Administration | Chola village self-government (Uttaramerur, kudavolai, variyams, sabha) as early participatory governance |
| Economy & trade | Chola Bay-of-Bengal maritime empire; Kakatiya tank irrigation and Motupalli port |
| Art & culture | Dravidian vimana, Chola bronzes (Nataraja), Hoysala stellate temples, Kakatiya toranas |
| Significance | Regional state formation; integration of Deccan and Tamil/Telugu identity |
| Limitations | Participation land-owning and caste-bound; dependence on feudatory nayakas; vulnerability to Delhi |

**Evidence to quote**
- Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c.919–921) — among the world's earliest records of elected local government.
- Three UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' (1987, extended 2004); Ramappa Temple inscribed UNESCO 2021.
- Rajendra I's Srivijaya naval expedition (c.1025) and missions to Song China — evidence of state-backed trade.
- Ganapati Deva's Abhaya Sasanam at Motupalli — a medieval charter protecting foreign merchants.
- Marco Polo's praise of Rudrama Devi's governance — a rare contemporary foreign testimony on a woman ruler.

**AP angle**
Kulottunga I united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (coastal Andhra) with the Cholas, carrying Chola administrative practice into the Telugu country; the Kakatiyas then gave the Telugu region its first political unity, irrigation network and the toranas now on Telangana's state emblem.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: contrast Chola elected sabhas with modern Panchayati Raj to show continuity of local self-government.
- Quote: Marco Polo on Rudrama Devi's just rule for the gender-and-governance angle.
- Diagram idea: a Deccan map marking Manyakheta, Thanjavur, Warangal, Belur/Halebidu and Devagiri to show the shift of power southward then its absorption by Delhi.
keyPoints: Mains M2-2 lens: analyse administration, art, economy, significance and limitations — not a ruler list.
Chola Uttaramerur self-government is the strongest 'early democracy' argument; link to Panchayati Raj.
Maritime economy: Rajendra I's Srivijaya expedition and China missions show state-backed trade.
AP angle: Kulottunga I's Vengi union and Kakatiya unification of the Telugu region (toranas on the state emblem).
Culture: three UNESCO Chola temples (1987/2004) and Ramappa Temple (UNESCO 2021) as evidence.
Limitation line: participation was land-owning and caste-bound; states leaned on feudatory nayakas.
